1.0.s.en: (1) John the Baptist and the Baptism of Christ

1.0.0.en: St. Matthew and St. Luke referred to some of the events connected with the bodily birth of Christ, and St. John referred to the divine birth of the Son from the Father. St. Mark, however, took a direct approach, declaring in his very first words that his book is the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, and he focused on the beginning of Christ's ministry, without mentioning any events that preceded it.

1.0.1.en: "Jesus": its meaning is "God saves"; its Hebrew origin is Yehoshua, which developed into Yeshua, and then "Jesus." This was the name of the Lord in His incarnation.

1.0.2.en: "Christ": that is, the One anointed as King, who is set apart for the salvation and renewal of mankind through its redemption on the Cross. "Son of God": that is, the name of divinity, which indicates the Godhead of the Word, the Son of God.

1.1.0.en: "As it is written": St. Mark refers to the prophecies (Mal 3:1; Isa 40:

1.1.1.en: 3) in the Old Testament, which pointed to the sending of John the Baptist as a messenger going before Christ the Savior, preparing souls to receive Him. In the Roman era, it was necessary for rulers or prominent persons to be preceded by someone who announced their coming. The world, in its corruption, was not ready to receive Christ, so God sent John to rebuke and to warn of the need for repentance, in order to prepare the way for Him.

1.1.2.en: "I send ... My messenger": the expression that Malachi used in his prophecy about John the Baptist.

1.1.3.en: "The voice of one crying": the expression that Isaiah used in his prophecy about John the Baptist, and it shows his crying out against evil and the wicked, calling for repentance.

1.2.0.en: The work that John did was to call people to repentance and to the forsaking of sin. It was the custom of the Jews to circumcise those among the Gentiles who converted to Judaism. In this way John changed that custom, and he used Baptism as a sign and a seal for the one who offered repentance (water being a symbol of washing and purity). The people responded to the call to repentance, and they went out to him from all places, and they were baptized.

1.3.0.en: "Camel's hair": a coarse, cheap garment worn by the poor, and worn also by the prophets, such as Elijah. It signifies detachment and the absence of love of money and its luxury.

1.3.1.en: "A girdle of a skin": as Elijah also wore (2 Kgs 1:8). It is a wide leather belt that tightens the waist, and it signifies striving and diligent work.

1.3.2.en: "He did eat locusts and wild honey": ... The locust is the well-known gnawing insect of the wilderness, and eating it was not forbidden (Lev 11:22), and the honey was the honey of bees found in the clefts of the rocks in the wilderness. Symbolically, it may be said that the locusts resemble the Jews who fell like insects in their sins, whereas repentance makes them sweet honey to Christ.

1.4.0.en: Besides his powerful call to repentance, he preached and prophesied about the coming of Christ. In humility, he made clear the difference between the two of them, placing himself in the position of the bent servant who loosens with his hand the thongs of his master's sandals. So the Lord lifted up that hand and placed it on His head at the Baptism, to teach us all that humility is the virtue that raises a person before God ... John also did not forget to make clear the difference between the baptism of water, which signifies cleansing, and the baptism of the Holy Spirit, which is founded on Christ.

1.4.1.en: My beloved friend, we cannot leave the figure of John without learning much from him:

1.4.2.en: First: he left the comfortable world for the desolate wilderness, which signifies evil, so that evil might be overcome by the call to repentance. Second: he was detached in his food, his drink and his clothing, so God gave him a peace, strength and courage that the world had not known. Third: despite his bold and powerful words, and his refusal to compromise with evil and his rebuking of the wicked, the crowds went out to him. So never be afraid to hold fast to the truth, whatever the evil around you, for it is God who works in you, and not we ourselves.

1.5.0.en: At the time appointed beforehand by God, Christ went to John at the river Jordan, to be baptized on behalf of sinful mankind, and not out of any need for repentance or cleansing.

1.5.1.en: "Nazareth of Galilee": the northern part of the land of Judea, and it is the place where Christ spent the days of His life from His return from Egypt as a child until the beginning of His preaching.

1.5.2.en: "Coming up out of the water": a clarification that Christ went down and came up, and for this reason our Church practices the sacrament of Baptism by immersion, and not by putting water on the head of the one being baptized; and the word "coming up" points to the resurrection from sin through Baptism.

1.5.3.en: "The heavens opened": the Baptism of Christ was accompanied by a declaration from heaven, and it was the first clear declaration to mankind of the doctrine of the Most Holy Trinity: the incarnate Son comes up from the water, the Holy Spirit takes the form of a dove and reveals Himself, and here is the Father declaring His eternal relationship with His Son, and that He is well pleased with His redemption of mankind. For this reason our Church considers the Feast of Epiphany a great feast of the Lord, and calls it by its theological name, "the Feast of the Divine Manifestation," because it is the declaration of the Most Holy Trinity.

1.6.s.en: (2) The temptation in the wilderness and the beginning of the preaching

1.6.0.en: In a clear indication of the Spirit's leading of the Christian after Baptism, the Lord went out into the wilderness of temptations, so that the believer may learn that the spiritual life will not be free of battles, but that we must overcome through Christ, as He overcame Satan. And despite the wild beasts, which signify the demons in their number and the variety of their warfare, the angels of the Lord minister to and guard His children who strive in His person. In this way God surrounds His Church with His care and concern, which keeps us and comforts us in our trials.

1.6.1.en: It is noted that St. Mark did not present the details of the spiritual battles throughout the forty days, but both Matthew and Luke spoke, in the fourth chapter of their Gospels, about the details of three of them, as an example of what Christ was exposed to of these battles.

1.7.0.en: "Now after that John was put in prison": that is, after Herod imprisoned John the Baptist, who used to oppose his evil by rebuking him, Christ began His ministry in Galilee, north of Judea (Nazareth and Capernaum), where He was first raised. In His wisdom, He did not begin in Jerusalem, so as not to clash with Herod or the chief priests. "The time is fulfilled": that is, the time had come for the fulfillment of all the prophecies written about Him in His incarnation and His redemption of man (Gen 49:10; Dan 9:24).

1.7.1.en: "The kingdom of God is at hand": that is, the beginning of the call to salvation and the clear manifestation of the glory of God, for the long-awaited Christ had come, and it is for man to declare his acceptance of this call through repentance and belief in the gospel of Christ. My Lord, my God and my Savior, You still call me to be Your son, to inherit the kingdom of life, and You laid down a condition for my obtaining it, which is my abiding always in repentance...

1.7.2.en: I beseech You, my God, give me also a repentant heart, steadfast in this repentance, for I do not want to lose my inheritance...

1.8.s.en: (3) The calling of some disciples and the healing of a demoniac in Capernaum

1.8.0.en: "The sea of Galilee": it is the same as the Sea of Tiberias and the Lake of Gennesaret, and it forms the eastern border of the land of Galilee.

1.8.1.en: "Simon and Andrew": fishermen, that is, from the simple folk, for God does not want the success of the ministry to be attributed to man's abilities, but to His own work through the simple, humble servant.

1.8.2.en: Their two names signified qualities that qualify a person for the service of God: Simon means the one who listens and obeys the word of God, and Andrew means "truly a man" ... that is, manliness and spiritual seriousness in service. "Come ye after me": that is, following Christ and imitating Him in all His attributes and teachings, for the faithful and influential servant is the one who makes Christ the leader of the whole course of his life, so that he takes from Him first in order to give to others second.

1.8.3.en: "They forsook their nets": their response was immediate, and they left whatever hindered them from following Christ, and this response means the following:

1.8.4.en: Their faith in Christ, their love for Him, their readiness to leave everything for His sake.

1.9.0.en: The same situation is repeated with James, whose name means "he who follows closely," pointing to the striving and struggle of the servant, and with John, whose name means "God is gracious to His creation." As Simon and Andrew did, they left their father in the ship with the hired servants, and went after Him, which indicates that they were among the wealthy who employed hired servants in fishing.

1.9.1.en: My dear friend, are you not ashamed with me before those who left everything to follow the good part? What then do we leave in this world for the sake of God? Let us begin with the least things, and God is able to set us over more afterward.

1.10.0.en: Capernaum was one of the largest cities of Galilee on the shore of the sea, and the synagogue was the place of worship where the Jews gathered for prayer and for the reading of the books of Moses and some of the prophecies. Synagogues were spread throughout the land of Judea, but there was only one temple, in Jerusalem, in which sacrifices were offered. "He taught": that is, He read some of the readings, and then gave the interpretation and the exhortation. His teaching was new, carrying spiritual influence and authority over those who listened, unlike the scribes, whose task was to teach and exhort the people at that time.

1.10.1.en: "The scribes": they trace their descent to Ezra the scribe, who is the most famous of those who collected and copied the holy books after some of the people returned from the captivity to Jerusalem, and the Book of Ezra was written in his name.

1.11.0.en: Present with the crowd in the synagogue was a man possessed by Satan, who could not bear the words of Christ, and who recognized His blessed person, and cried out in great alarm: I know You, You are the Holy One, the Son of God, in whose hand alone is the authority to destroy us.

1.11.1.en: "And Jesus rebuked him": that is, He reproved him firmly, and commanded him to be silent and to come out of this man. This shows the absolute authority of the Lord Christ over the whole kingdom of evil and of the demons, and that Christ does not accept testimony from Satan even if it is true, for there is no fellowship of light with darkness.

1.12.0.en: In Satan's last desperate attempts, he threw the man down in a faint, but he could do nothing but come out and obey the command of Christ. The coming out of this demon had a profound effect on those who watched from among the crowd, so they marveled, asking about the person of Christ Himself, "What is this?" Then they marveled also at the manner of His teaching, at which they were astonished and had never heard the like before, and finally they were amazed at His authority over the unclean spirits, the like of which they had never seen, as they saw the demon come out at one word from His mouth.

1.12.1.en: And of course this event had a great effect, so its report spread, not only in Capernaum, but in all the villages of the region of Galilee and the surrounding area.

1.13.s.en: (4) The healing of Peter's mother-in-law and the preaching in the cities of Galilee

1.13.0.en: "The house of Simon and Andrew": Christ came out of the synagogue and went with the four disciples to the house of Simon and his brother Andrew, and this house was in Capernaum, and some hold that the house of Simon Peter was the one where Christ always stayed when He visited Capernaum.

1.14.0.en: Simon's mother-in-law, who lived with him, had been taken with a great fever. When they told Him of this, He had compassion on her and raised her up, taking her by the hand. In this regard St. Luke says (4:39), "He rebuked the fever, and it left her: and immediately she arose and ministered unto them."

1.14.1.en: And this, beloved, teaches us two things:

1.14.2.en: (1) That we ask of Christ not only for our own illnesses, but we also pray for the sufferings of others, as the household of Simon's mother-in-law did, and as the Church teaches us when she prays for the sick in all her prayers. (2) That the woman, when she was healed, offered thanks by serving everyone. So thanking God is not words only, but deeds also.

1.15.0.en: "At even, when the sun did set": ... out of respect for the commandment of the Sabbath and not traveling during it, the people waited until the Sabbath ended with the setting of the sun, and then gathered around the house, desiring the healing of their sick, or to see the miracles of healing, and healing was accomplished for great numbers, as was also the casting out of unclean spirits.

1.15.1.en: "He suffered not the devils to speak": ... Christ always did so, because He does not accept testimony about Himself from Satan (see v. 25).

1.16.0.en: "In the morning ... a solitary place": that is, at the dawn of Sunday, before anyone had risen ... and the purpose of the solitary place was that no one should see or hear Him.

1.16.1.en: Christ teaches us and gives us a model of quiet prayer in which a person is alone with God, and withdraws with Him to speak with Him and rejoice in meeting Him.

1.16.2.en: And if Christ, my friend, being without sin, prays ... how much more do we need, we who are burdened with sins and cares, to stand before God to obtain our rest?!

1.17.0.en: Because of Christ's absence from the house when the four disciples awoke, they searched for Him. And when they found Him, they told Him that there were many people seeking Him (in Capernaum). But Christ, who came forth from heaven for the preaching and the proclaiming of the Kingdom, let nothing hinder Him, so He told the disciples that He must go to the surrounding villages to complete His work.

1.17.1.en: And here we learn from the Lord Christ a useful lesson, which is that we should not let crowding or insistence make us forget our spiritual goals, for how many hindrances we shall meet ... so do not allow them, beloved, to turn your gaze away from your spiritual work or your eternity.

1.18.0.en: At first Christ was permitted to enter the synagogues of the Jews in Galilee, but on His later visits, after the slanders of the priests and the leaders of the Jews, He was forbidden to preach and teach in the synagogues. It is noted thereby that faith in Him, after the acceptance of His teaching in the synagogues, was what cast out the demons ... for faith always precedes healing.

1.19.0.en: The leprous man came worshiping the person of Christ with respect and humility. Despite his hope and his need for healing, he teaches us an important lesson in how to ask of God, for he knelt and said to Him: "If thou wilt," that is, "Let Your will be done."

1.19.1.en: Despite our confidence in God's ability to answer all our requests, we must put the will of Christ above our need, because He knows what is right and best for us.

1.20.0.en: "Moved with compassion ... and touched him": St. Mark reveals to us the disposition of the heart of Christ, filled with tenderness toward His creation, for although the word of Christ alone was enough to heal him, He touched him with His hand, a feeling of which this man had been deprived, since the Law forbade touching a leper because of his uncleanness. So the touch of the hand came tenderly upon this body, which had forgotten the meaning of being gently patted by another for a long time. And at the moment in which Christ said "I will," the leprosy departed from him and he was cleansed.

1.20.1.en: And this teaches us that when we feel aversion toward some person, we should remember the tenderness of Christ toward the leper, and His tenderness toward us sinners.

1.21.0.en: "And He straitly charged him": what is meant is not rebuking the man, upon whom He had had compassion, but rather that He obliged him not to return to the sin that had been the cause of his illness, and also obliged him to go to the priest, who, according to the Law, examines and declares the healing, and receives the sacrifices that he must offer.

1.21.1.en: And it is noted here that although the healing was completed, Christ respected the order that God had established, and the role of the priest in it, as it is stated in the Book of Leviticus (chs. 13, 14), that when a leper was healed, he had to go to the priest for examination, and then offer a thank offering in the temple.

1.21.2.en: Likewise we can say that this is what happens in the sacrament of repentance and confession: the person comes to Christ kneeling and acknowledging his sins, and He says to him: I take them away from you. But go and show yourself to the priest, and offer there the sacrifice of your confession.

1.21.3.en: "See thou say nothing to any man": that is, do not boast of your healing, claiming that your righteousness was the cause of it, but keep your humility.

1.21.4.en: May we, my beloved brother, learn to surround God's private dealings with us with some care and secrecy, lest we be afflicted with pride and conceit ... and make your father of confession your reference in this.

1.22.0.en: But the man, because of his great joy and excitement, spread the news of his healing in all places, until the fame of the Lord Jesus spread in the surrounding country, and He was not able to enter it because of the crowding, so He stayed in the desert places so that everyone could meet Him.

1.22.1.en: The healing of the paralytic, the calling of Matthew, and confrontations with the scribes and Pharisees
